constructs.nearest: Its nearest neighbor is Abstraction level shift, since both have a side that covers more ground, but abstraction covers ground with one superordinate word while this construct covers it by distributing mass over many sibling words, and a narrow cluster of specific words is narrow without being abstract.

constructs.name: Same referent, rival synonyms
constructs.definition: Both sides name the same thing throughout and differ only in which member of an interchangeable naming set they favor, so the difference is lexical selection under a constant referent rather than any change in what is being talked about.
constructs.nearest: Its nearest neighbor is Explicit versus sanitized, because both describe rival words competing for one slot, but here the referent never changes and neither side supplies a permitted substitute, so what varies is register or idiom rather than whether the thing is named at all.

constructs.name: Lateral referent swap
constructs.definition: The entity that the action applies to is exchanged for an entity of a different category but comparable ordinariness, so the difference lies in which class of thing occupies the slot and not in whether either class is permitted.

constructs.name: Abstraction level shift
constructs.definition: One side prefers words naming particular instances while the other prefers the superordinate category word that covers them, so the difference is the taxonomic level at which the same field is named.
constructs.nearest: Its nearest neighbor is Wide scatter, tight cluster; it is not that one because the change described is in the level of the individual word rather than in how many words share the probability mass, and a set of particular names can be just as small as the category word that subsumes them.

constructs.name: Modifiers follow their head
constructs.definition: The observable difference is carried by grammatically dependent words that are pulled along by whatever the item they modify has become, so the contrast surfaces in a satellite word class rather than in the item that actually changed.
constructs.nearest: Its nearest neighbor is Explicit versus sanitized, since the modifiers ride on exactly that substitution, but the claim being made is about which grammatical category registers the shift, and the modifiers themselves are not marked or unmarked in the way the head words are.

constructs.name: Grammatical form, same word
constructs.definition: One lexical item appears on both sides in different grammatical constructions, one of which projects further material after it and the other of which stands alone, so the difference is syntactic frame rather than content.
constructs.nearest: Its nearest neighbor is Same referent, rival synonyms, because both hold the referent fixed and vary only the wording, but a possessive and a bare form are one word in two frames rather than two competing words, and the contrast here predicts what comes next in the string.

result.topic_audit: The usual test is degenerate for this batch: all twenty-one descriptions quote words that fit one and the same frame, something like a person beginning to stroke his something, so shared topic is universal here and cannot by itself distinguish a construct from a topic. What does the work instead is that the sub-topics inside that frame cut across my constructs rather than lining up with them. Genital vocabulary appears in Explicit versus sanitized, in Same referent rival synonyms, and in Modifiers follow their head; facial hair appears in Explicit versus sanitized (r096d02f, r7a8495d, rf69eb30) and again in Wide scatter tight cluster (r03e1490, rc203b05, rea44798); animals appear in four different constructs (r257f2ac and rf69eb30 as sanitized substitutes, r17d1e06 as a lateral swap, r61d8d3d as an abstraction contrast); relational nouns for people appear in Explicit versus sanitized, in Lateral referent swap, and in Grammatical form same word. Construct by construct: Explicit versus sanitized shares no single sub-topic, since its innocuous side is variously beards, hands, pets, relatives, and torsos, and I am confident it is a construct because what its members agree on is the markedness asymmetry, not the substitute. Wide scatter tight cluster does lean toward one sub-topic, the beard and chin region, in three of its four members, and this is the one I am least sure of; I keep it because r97dba1f's tight side is explicit genital words rather than facial hair, which shows the shape claim can be made with the sub-topic removed, but a fourth member from a different sentence would settle it and I do not have one. Same referent rival synonyms shares a sub-topic outright, both members being about slang for the same body part, and I hold it as a construct because the defining move, holding the referent constant while shuffling the name, is stated in both and is exactly what the largest construct never does; still, with two same-topic members it is the second one I would want challenged. Lateral referent swap shares no sub-topic, its two members involving animals and kin terms respectively. The three single-member constructs cannot share a topic with themselves, and each was kept because its claim is about a mechanism (dependent-word tracking, syntactic frame, taxonomic level) that no other description makes.
result.notes: Three things a reader should know about how I grouped. First, direction is not treated as part of construct identity. Most members of Explicit versus sanitized put the explicit vocabulary on A, but r7e14d30 and rd6b0e81 put it on B, and since the raters saw different sentences and were given no vocabulary or orientation convention, I cannot tell whether that flip is a real reversal of the underlying pair or just a difference in which list a rater called A; grouping on the axis and recording the polarity separately seemed more honest than making two constructs whose only difference might be labeling. Second, several descriptions carry two claims and I assigned each to one construct on the strength of the name its author gave it and its opening clause, not by taking a vote over the words quoted. The clearest cases are r257f2ac, which reports both explicit-to-innocuous substitution and a scatter of the innocuous side across four different categories, and rea44798 and r97dba1f, which report both breadth and explicitness; if multiple membership were permitted, r257f2ac would belong in Wide scatter tight cluster as well, and rea44798 and r97dba1f would belong in Explicit versus sanitized as well. Third, Explicit versus sanitized has ten members and is the obvious candidate for a split. The split I considered and rejected was between descriptions where the unmarked side reconstructs a whole coherent alternative situation (r096d02f, rf69eb30, and to a degree r257f2ac) and descriptions that merely report which vocabulary sits on each side (rb789759, r3f48db3, r7a8495d, r7bd919f). I rejected it because that distinction tracks how expansively each rater chose to narrate what they saw rather than a difference in the relation they identified, and I would not defend it to someone who thought it was one construct.

Transgressive to permitted substitution is the group where that risk bites hardest, because all eleven members quote explicit sexual vocabulary and someone could fairly say I have merely collected the descriptions that mention genitals; what persuades me it is a construct is that four other descriptions quote exactly the same vocabulary and are not in it (r4e43116 and rbde40e6 quote the same words but hold the referent constant, r2a2661b quotes only the modifiers attached to those words, r97dba1f quotes them but names concentration as the relation), so membership is decided by the relation and not by the lexicon. Broad field, narrow cluster shares the body-part vocabulary among its three members, but two of them run in opposite directions (rc203b05 goes broad-to-narrow and r03e1490 narrow-to-broad) and one of them, r97dba1f, is about where the weight piles up rather than which region is covered, so the shared subject is doing no work in holding them together. Instance to category label stands alone and is about animals, which is also r17d1e06's subject matter and yet the two are in different constructs, which is the cleanest evidence in this batch that I am not sorting by topic. Reassigned licit object is the group I am least sure of: both members involve relational nouns for people, and I am grouping them on the claim that a shift from animal to spouse and a shift from kin to romantic partner are the same kind of move among equally permitted objects, which is defensible but would be much easier to test against a batch drawn from other sentences. Synonym pool reallocation is the second one I flag, since both its members concern the same synonym set and I have nothing outside that set to show the construct generalizes. Modifiers follow heads and Construction over content each have one member and no topic to share.

result.topic_audit: The usual test is degenerate for this batch: all twenty-one descriptions quote words that fit one and the same frame, something like a person beginning to stroke his something, so shared topic is universal here and cannot by itself distinguish a construct from a topic. What does the work instead is that the sub-topics inside that frame cut across my constructs rather than lining up with them. Genital vocabulary appears in Explicit versus sanitized, in Same referent rival synonyms, and in Modifiers follow their head; facial hair appears in Explicit versus sanitized (r096d02f, r7a8495d, rf69eb30) and again in Wide scatter tight cluster (r03e1490, rc203b05, rea44798); animals appear in four different constructs (r257f2ac and rf69eb30 as sanitized substitutes, r17d1e06 as a lateral swap, r61d8d3d as an abstraction contrast); relational nouns for people appear in Explicit versus sanitized, in Lateral referent swap, and in Grammatical form same word. Construct by construct: Explicit versus sanitized shares no single sub-topic, since its innocuous side is variously beards, hands, pets, relatives, and torsos, and I am confident it is a construct because what its members agree on is the markedness asymmetry, not the substitute. Wide scatter tight cluster does lean toward one sub-topic, the beard and chin region, in three of its four members, and this is the one I am least sure of; I keep it because r97dba1f's tight side is explicit genital words rather than facial hair, which shows the shape claim can be made with the sub-topic removed, but a fourth member from a different sentence would settle it and I do not have one. Same referent rival synonyms shares a sub-topic outright, both members being about slang for the same body part, and I hold it as a construct because the defining move, holding the referent constant while shuffling the name, is stated in both and is exactly what the largest construct never does; still, with two same-topic members it is the second one I would want challenged. Lateral referent swap shares no sub-topic, its two members involving animals and kin terms respectively. The three single-member constructs cannot share a topic with themselves, and each was kept because its claim is about a mechanism (dependent-word tracking, syntactic frame, taxonomic level) that no other description makes.
result.notes: Three things a reader should know about how I grouped. First, direction is not treated as part of construct identity. Most members of Explicit versus sanitized put the explicit vocabulary on A, but r7e14d30 and rd6b0e81 put it on B, and since the raters saw different sentences and were given no vocabulary or orientation convention, I cannot tell whether that flip is a real reversal of the underlying pair or just a difference in which list a rater called A; grouping on the axis and recording the polarity separately seemed more honest than making two constructs whose only difference might be labeling. Second, several descriptions carry two claims and I assigned each to one construct on the strength of the name its author gave it and its opening clause, not by taking a vote over the words quoted. The clearest cases are r257f2ac, which reports both explicit-to-innocuous substitution and a scatter of the innocuous side across four different categories, and rea44798 and r97dba1f, which report both breadth and explicitness; if multiple membership were permitted, r257f2ac would belong in Wide scatter tight cluster as well, and rea44798 and r97dba1f would belong in Explicit versus sanitized as well. Third, Explicit versus sanitized has ten members and is the obvious candidate for a split. The split I considered and rejected was between descriptions where the unmarked side reconstructs a whole coherent alternative situation (r096d02f, rf69eb30, and to a degree r257f2ac) and descriptions that merely report which vocabulary sits on each side (rb789759, r3f48db3, r7a8495d, r7bd919f). I rejected it because that distinction tracks how expansively each rater chose to narrate what they saw rather than a difference in the relation they identified, and I would not defend it to someone who thought it was one construct.

result.topic_audit: Constructs 1 (politeness-to-force), 2 (informing versus requesting) and 4 (remaining versus departing) are built almost entirely from descriptions whose quoted words overlap heavily (asked, told, demanded, requested, resigned, quit), which is exactly the shared-vocabulary signature the task warns produces topic clusters rather than constructs. I kept them separate because each names a different logical relation among that shared vocabulary, and, tellingly, different raters sort the SAME words onto different sides depending on which relation they are naming: construct 1's raters put informed/announced with the calm pole; construct 4's rcfe51b7 puts announced with the exit pole instead; construct 2's raters put asked/requested with demanded, against informing. That cross-sorting of identical words is evidence the three name different relations rather than one topic wearing three labels, but confidence stays medium: with the underlying sentences hidden by design, I cannot rule out that some of this apparent diversity is noise from raters describing near-identical distributions in different words rather than three real axes. Constructs 5 (acting versus merely being), 6 (generic versus elaborated diction), 8 (verbal versus physical violence) and 9 (direction of transfer) are higher confidence: each turns on a formal or grammatical property of the verbs -- transitivity, synonym density/register, a crossing into a different kind of action, or the direction of an already-shared transaction -- rather than on a narrative theme, and construct 6 specifically pairs descriptions of two different actions (reporting-type verbs and handover-type verbs) under one diction-register logic, which is the cross-topic pairing the task is asking us to find. Constructs 3, 7 and 10 are singletons that share surface vocabulary with constructs 1/2/4 (desperation and charge language overlaps demand/confront language); I would not be surprised if they collapsed into a larger construct with more data, though each currently rests on an explicit definitional claim its nearest neighbor does not make (bridging two emotional registers, or naming a channel rather than a force level). Construct 11 is the one I trust least: its strongest evidence duplicates construct 6 exactly (gave versus presented/delivered/handed), and it may be construct 6 plus topic-driven noise from the same underlying scenario rather than a genuinely separate third construct.

result.topic_audit:
Nearly every word across all 22 descriptions belongs to one recognizable domain: a person confronting, informing, or leaving in a dispute with another party, often over money or employment (demanded, resigned, quit, fired, tendered, and so on). That is a real limitation on this whole exercise. The instructions describe many different sentences on many different subjects, but the vocabulary in front of me never actually leaves that one domain, so I cannot rule out that some or all of the 22 come from a single underlying sentence measured or sampled in different ways, in which case these constructs are different axes through one distribution rather than fully topic-independent generalizations.

Within that limitation, construct by construct: Stay-confront vs. exit, Politeness vs. force, Register formality, and Informing vs. requesting all draw their members from what reads as the same narrow scene, so I am not fully confident these are constructs rather than restatements of one topic under different emphases. I kept them separate because each names a different logical relation between the two sides (remain-or-leave; polite-or-forceful; plain-or-formal; state-or-request) that would still make sense as a distinct question in an unrelated scene, and none of the four reduces to another by substituting synonyms.

Violence intrusion and Action vs. bodily stasis are the two I am most confident name real constructs rather than a shared topic: their defining move (one violent verb spiking in rank; body-position verbs displacing transactional ones) is a structural pattern in a ranked word list, not a description of what the scene is about, and would be recognizable in a list about any two people in any setting.

Giving vs. taking and Direct vs. institutional address are singletons drawn from the same scene's handover and reporting vocabulary respectively, but each names an axis (direction of a transfer; audience of an utterance) that is a general property of any two-party exchange, not specific to this one.

Flat vs. charged affect and Distress vs. composure both sit close enough to Politeness vs. force that a stricter reader could fold all three into one coarser "emotional intensity" construct. I kept them apart because each specifies a different opposition (force against calm; any charge against flatness; distress against composure), but I hold this three-way split with less confidence than the others, and flag it as the most defensible place to merge if a second rater disagreed.
result.notes: Two boundary cases worth flagging explicitly: r5653d01 was placed under Informing vs. requesting rather than Stay-confront vs. exit even though its own name mentions "exiting," because five of its six A-words are informing-type and only one (resigned) is an exit word. r99facdf was placed under Register formality rather than Stay-confront vs. exit for the same reason: its own name says "blunt exit," but only one A-word (quit) is exit vocabulary while the B-side has none, and the rater's stated contrast (bluntness vs. the adverb "calmly") is about manner, not about staying or leaving. Both calls are defensible but not forced by the data; a stricter reading could move either one. File read only; no other files opened and no commands run, per the task's own instruction and the launching agent's constraint.

result.topic_audit:
Controlled vs explosive manner (5 members, the largest group) does not share a narrative topic across members: "measured reprimand vs explosive outburst," "loud aggression vs controlled interrogation," and "hostile outburst vs calm reasoned communication" invoke different implied scenes (a phone call, an interrogation, a confrontation) with only partially overlapping vocabulary, converging on the composure axis alone. Confident this is a construct.

Reprimand intensity gradient (3 members) shares some vocabulary (yell, scream, berate, lecture recur across members) but the members disagree on which specific words count as more vs less intense, so the shared element is the existence of a graded scale, not a shared word set. All three do stay within one broad domain (criticism/reprimand language) without crossing into calm speech, threat, or physical action -- this is the large cluster I am least confident is fully topic-free, since "reprimand" itself could be read as a topic rather than a structural axis.

Idiomatic vs literal naming (3 members) spans distinct apparent scenes (a formal interrogation, a scolding, a violent-sounding confrontation) and the idiom vocabulary in each member does not overlap at all (grill/lay; tear/chew/lay; beat/thrash/hurl/unleash) -- good evidence the shared element is grammatical form, not topic.

Semantic narrowing vs breadth (2 members) draws its "broad" side from different categories in each case (calm speech + threat + emotion in one; ordinary action + violence in the other), so the shared element is structural (how many categories a list spans) rather than which categories. Confident.

The six one-member constructs (coercive content suppressed, expressive vs propositional speech, one-way vs reciprocal address, real words vs redaction, venting vs differentiated response, setting-linked formality shift) cannot be topic-audited comparatively -- each is trusted on the strength of the mechanism its single description names, which is the most exposed position in this exercise since there is no second instance to confirm the axis would survive a change of subject matter.

result.topic_audit: All 24 descriptions sample completions of what appears to be one underlying prompt, so heavy vocabulary overlap across constructs is expected and was treated as uninformative on its own; the audit below asks, for each construct, whether its members' shared subject matter is doing the classifying work instead of the stated relation. Two constructs pass this test cleanly and are the ones I trust most: "Generic vs specific granularity" pairs a description drawn from one category (a body-part term) with a description drawn from an unrelated category (a dwelling term), which is exactly the cross-topic pairing that would be impossible if topic were secretly organizing the grouping; "Function word vs noun" isolates a grammatical class (bare prepositions) that shares essentially no vocabulary with any other construct's members, so its coherence cannot be a topic artifact. "Two-term concrete swap," "Marked term, pooled alternative," "Veiled vs open reference," "Concrete-abstract pole reversal," "Faculty vs poetic idiom," and "Private vs public/figurative" all draw on the same small pool of body/space/emotion vocabulary as "Literal vs. figurative reach" and each other; I am reasonably confident each names a real, checkable difference in how its members pair or pool that vocabulary (stated explicitly above in each "nearest" note), but I flag three as genuinely unsure rather than confidently distinct: "Faculty vs poetic idiom" could plausibly be read as a finer subdivision of "Literal vs. figurative reach" rather than a separate construct, since all four of its words already sit inside that construct's undifferentiated figurative pole; "Private vs public/figurative" rests on a single description and could likewise be one rater's idiosyncratic framing of the same territory "Literal vs. figurative reach" and "Marked term, pooled alternative" already cover; and within "Affective charge in modifiers," the third member (raddba30) is a hybrid that mixes gentleness-adverbs with abstract/euphemistic nouns, and could arguably belong nearer "Literal vs. figurative reach" or "Veiled vs open reference" instead. "Archaic-to-plain register" and "Set diversity narrowing" share vocabulary with their neighbors but state a claim (word age/formality; set size and heterogeneity) that is orthogonal to topic, so I am confident in both despite each having only one member.

result.topic_audit:
Every one of the fourteen descriptions in this file appears to derive from the same single sentence, a person being disciplined at work after repeated write-ups, deciding whether to leave, comply, or push back. That is unusual against the task's own framing, which describes raters looking at "many different sentences on many different subjects" that the reader is not told apart; within this one file, by content, there is only one subject. That makes the topic-audit's normal discriminating test (does the same relation recur across a different topic, and does the same topic split into different relations) impossible to run in its strong form here, since there is no second topic in the file to check against. What I can still show is that the six constructs are not merely six restatements of "this is about quitting a job," and I take each in turn.

Formal register of exit (r31bfd4e, r3f968a7): both members share the topic, but the confidence the grouping is a construct rather than a topic-echo rests on a check available inside the file itself: several other descriptions elsewhere (Withdrawal versus confrontation, Decisive exit softened) also use the word "resign," but assign it to the opposite side of their own A/B split, or pair it with unrelated words like "retire" and "stay." If the same lexical item marks opposite relations depending on which description it appears in, the grouping here is tracking a stated relation (informal-to-formal restatement of one act), not a shared vocabulary item.

Generic versus scenario-specific diction (r41083a9, r5dcda9f, r7edaf2e, r7ff5dfe, rd4ca354): five independent raters, using five different vocabularies for it (context-generic/context-responsive, generic/idiomatic, generic/named-transition, generic/context-relevant), converge on the same claim, that probability mass moves from words unconnected to the prompt toward words the prompt specifically motivates. That is the axis the task warns is easy to miss under a topic sort: this construct would show up in a file about an entirely unrelated sentence, wherever a generic-verb list is compared against a prompt-anchored one, so I am confident in it. The one soft spot is r5dcda9f, whose "idiomatic" framing edges toward the hedging-collapse construct; I kept it here because its stated contrast is still generic-versus-specific, with idiom as the specific pole's flavor rather than a separate claim.

Withdrawal versus confrontation (r22d0464, r6b58c8f, rb3e40f1): shares the topic. I am least confident about r22d0464's place in this group: its B side (file, write, take, put, change) is more generic-sounding than rb3e40f1's explicitly adversarial set (confront, fight, keep, talk, tell, try), and it is only "file" that carries the confrontational reading (as in filing a grievance) rather than the whole set. result.topic_audit: All 21 descriptions sit within one surface register -- an institution's response to a complaint -- so at the coarsest grain every construct's members appear to share a topic, and this is the trap the instructions warn about. The evidence that the groupings track structure rather than that shared surface is the instability of individual words across constructs: an admission-type word (e.g. admitted) is grouped as an outcome-word in 'consequence named vs withheld' and as a talk-word (opposed to concrete action) in 'resolving act vs mere talk'; an offer-type word is a noncommittal generic verb in one construct and a concrete remedy in another; investigatory verbs are fused with conciliatory verbs into one pole in 'personnel action vs any response' but opposed to them in 'consequence named vs withheld'. A grouping driven by topic would keep such words together; these constructs instead split them, which is what licenses calling them constructs. Two are flagged as unsure. 'Bureaucratic vs apologetic register' (r6c8037c, ra9a92a9) sits close enough to 'consequence named vs withheld' that one member's own gloss uses outcome-language, and a reader could defensibly merge them; I kept them apart on the strength of where each rater's own emphasis fell (genericness of the verb vs. presence of a named outcome), not on a difference I can independently verify. 'Personnel action vs any response' (r2397b9b) is a genuine hybrid of 'consequence named vs withheld' and 'staff action vs complainant address'; its single-member status reflects that no second instance of exactly its blend turned up, not confidence that it is irreducibly sui generis. 'Adverb anchor, unstable verbs' (r645a540, rad856fb) is the one construct I am least sure is real: the two members' own accompanying verb clusters contradict each other in valence, which could mean the temporal adverb is a genuine shared organizing feature the raters both caught, or could mean both raters independently imposed a tidy temporal narrative on a noisier, non-temporal underlying split -- the file gives no way to distinguish these from the descriptions alone.
result.notes: I read only the named file and ran no commands, per the file's own instructions. I did not attempt to infer which of the 21 descriptions came from which underlying sentence, as instructed. Second, 12 constructs from 21 descriptions is a moderate degree of splitting; I deliberately did not collapse the four or five constructs that all loosely involve 'commitment vs. process' into one mega-bucket, because in each case the specific words that carry the signal are assigned inconsistently across those constructs, which I read as evidence they are tracking distinct (if related) oppositions rather than one construct redescribed. A different, defensible reading could merge 'consequence named vs withheld', 'bureaucratic vs apologetic register', and 'any definite stance vs vague' into a single broader construct; I kept them separate and said why in each 'nearest' field rather than presenting the split as settled.

result.topic_audit: All 21 descriptions share one surface subject matter (a hospital's response to a complaint) because the file bundles many underlying sentences that differ only in the specific harm complained about, a variable invisible to the two word lists being compared -- so surface-topic overlap across every construct here is expected and is not by itself evidence of topic-conflation.
